title: From Sweeping Floors to 20,000 Cups a Day: The Remarkable Story of Café Niloufer's Babu Rao
excerpt: A. Babu Rao arrived in Hyderabad with nothing, worked as a cleaner at a small tea café, and built it into India's largest chai chain — one kadak cup at a time.
body:
• A. Babu Rao arrived in Hyderabad from a small village in Adilabad with nothing, sleeping on railway station platforms before finding work as a cleaner at a tea café.
  • He rose from sweeper to waiter to kitchen worker, eventually managing the entire café by 1978 and purchasing it outright in 1993.
  • Under his ownership, Café Niloufer grew from serving 400 cups a day to over 20,000, expanding from a single Lakdikapul outlet to multiple locations including HITEC City and Hyderabad Airport.
  • Now operating as ABR Cafe & Bakers Private Limited with over 1,000 employees, Café Niloufer is recognized as India's largest chai café chain.

A Boy From Adilabad With Nothing to Lose

A. Babu Rao was born into a poor family in a small village in Telangana's Adilabad district. During his school years in Maharashtra, he helped out at his uncle's shop. One moment from that period would shape his life forever: his father sold the family's cow to pay for his schoolbooks. Understanding the depth of that sacrifice, Babu Rao resolved to make something of himself.

After finishing school, he returned to Hyderabad with no money and no connections. He slept on the platform at Secunderabad railway station, took whatever small jobs he could find, and eventually landed at a modest café near Niloufer Hospital in Lakdikapul — not as a cook or a waiter, but as a cleaner.

From Broom to Business

The café took its name from the hospital next door, and in the mid-1970s it was a modest establishment serving tea and biscuits to locals. Babu Rao swept floors and washed dishes. But he moved up quickly — first to waiting tables, then to preparing the biscuits and tea that drew customers in.

"I realised early on that chai is an essential and it is one thing people consume multiple times in a day and yet want the taste to remain the same. I have ensured that it remains so."

— A. Babu Rao, speaking to The Hindu

By 1978, Babu Rao had signed an agreement to manage the entire café. He paid a fixed monthly amount to the original owners and kept the profits. The arrangement worked. He blended his own tea powder to achieve a specific color, consistency, and flavor — a recipe he has maintained for decades. Initially, the café sold around 400 cups a day. Under his management, that number would eventually climb to 20,000.

Purchasing the Dream

For 15 years, Babu Rao ran the café while saving every rupee he could. In 1993, he had enough to buy the business outright. Ownership allowed him to expand both the menu and the operation. The café became famous for its kadak Irani chai served in ceramic cups, Osmania biscuits baked fresh an hour before serving, malai buns, and bun maska.

To this day, Babu Rao is the first person to sample the chai each morning — arriving at 4:30 AM to taste and give feedback, ensuring the flavor meets his exacting standard.

Building India's Largest Chai Chain

What started as a single roadside café has grown into a chain with outlets in prominent Hyderabad neighborhoods including HITEC City, Banjara Hills, Himayathnagar, and Rajiv Gandhi International Airport. The company now operates as ABR Cafe & Bakers Private Limited and employs between 1,000 and 5,000 people, according to its LinkedIn profile.

The menu has expanded over the years to include vegetarian rice combos, millet-based dishes, and a retail line of Niloufer tea blends for home preparation. But the core offering — the chai-and-biscuit combination that made the café famous — remains unchanged.

A Hyderabadi Institution

For generations of Hyderabadis, Niloufer is more than a café. It is where students cram before exams, where friends catch up over roadside gossip, where families return year after year for a Rs 12 cup of tea that tastes exactly the way they remember it.

"My grandfather moved to this area in the early 90s and started having Niloufer chai," one regular told The Better India. "Later, my father and his friends started hanging out there. And now, my friends and I go there. Going to Niloufer Cafe is a tradition passed down in the family."

Babu Rao, who now drives a high-end car and uses an iPhone, has never forgotten where he came from. His story — from a boy who slept on a railway platform to the owner of India's largest chai chain — remains the first thing regulars tell newcomers as the aroma of freshly brewed Irani chai fills the air.
image_caption: A. Babu Rao at Café Niloufer in Hyderabad, the tea chain he built from a single outlet into India's largest chai café. The business now spans multiple locations across the city, including HITEC City and Hyderabad Airport.
nri_angle: Café Niloufer's Irani chai is a taste of home for Hyderabadi NRIs worldwide, and Babu Rao's rags-to-riches story resonates with the Indian immigrant experience.
